summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This session continued a long-running computational physics project called the Löwdin project, which aims to derive ionization energies for elements across the periodic table from first principles using a chain of physical mechanisms (relativistic corrections, exchange, self-interaction correction, spin-orbit coupling, and correlation energy) with no fitted constants. The session opened with a full archive restoration: LOWDIN-HANDOFF-30 was extracted, verified (630/630 files), the runtime rebuilt from layered packs 18–31, three C kernels compiled, and all 45 standing gates passed before any new work began.

The session executed five items in order. First, the spin-dependence of the second-order exchange constant E0B(ζ) was resolved by a scaling argument and confirmed via Loos–Gill 2011: E0B is exactly ζ-independent, requiring no code change. Second, fifteen chain rows were run under both correlation forms R (full RPA ring plus bare second-order exchange) and Z (truncated high-density expansion) with a new corr='R' hook added to t7c_corrz.py; the R/Z shift ratio proved class-resolved and ordered by orbital diffuseness (4f 1.16, 3d 1.18, nd≥4 1.41, 6s 2.32), but the comparison was not decisive at the 0.002 level. Third, Sc's Janak quadrature flag was closed by running eps(f=1e-3), reducing the gap from 1.2e-3 to 8.7e-5. Fourth, a fault was registered against a prior finding: form R never overbinds the benchmark UEG — both R and Z underbind from the same side — withdrawing an earlier inference that the d-row object was non-local. Fifth, an entrant-weighted r_s analysis showed R and Z are one local correlation object sampled at two truncation orders, with the per-subshell trigger being the entrant's correlation-weighted r_s (4f ~0.4, 3d ~0.7–1.2, nd≥4 ~1.9–2.1, 6s ~6.8); the nd≥4 local shortfall under R matches the size of the d-row object (Y +0.0051, Lu +0.0038 Ha), indicating the object is mostly a local screened-exchange deficiency rather than a non-local effect.

The session also addressed two conceptual questions from the person. On whether R and Z represent two parts of one mechanism triggered per subshell: confirmed, but the branching coordinate is not n+ℓ but rather (n−ℓ−1, ℓ) — node count and centrifugal index — already the chain's own labels. On whether element Z+1 can be derived from element Z as a tree of mechanisms rooted at hydrogen: partially confirmed as the oldest idea in the field (Bohr 1922 through Berengut), with the walk test (LCP3 Rule B, T0 ruling LCP10) identified as a standing target; a spec was written but the computation was gated behind the correlation form being closed first. On Maxwell's equations: identified as already implicit in three places (Coulomb as Gauss's law, spin-orbit as Ampère–Faraday, RPA ring as the Lindhard dielectric function), with the candidate third correlation form (ring plus Lindhard-screened second-order exchange) framed as "let the Pauli term see the field the gas has already dressed," and the f-sum and compressibility sum rules noted as additional gates. The session sealed LOWDIN-HANDOFF-31 (656 files, manifest ok=656 bad=0, fresh-extract recipe verified), with SPEC-SOSEX and SPEC-WALK written for the next session. A foreign-file check fault (F31.4) was registered and corrected: the open-time check had been read through a truncated listing; a census-to-file confirmed rt/ is clean.

R 1649's tier census (A 218 · B 157 · C 179) is contaminated at 55%.** *THE INDEX WAS NOT TOUCHED BY IT: zero single-n rows are witnessed, because R 1651's keyability criterion excluded them — as a side-effect, not by design. ### 1667

**§H.10 — THE HANDOFF IS BEGUN AT 90%, NOT AT EXHAUSTION.** *M's Prime Handoff Directive: state when the context window reaches 90% and recommend handoff then.* **§H TOLD A SESSION HOW TO HAND OFF AND WHAT MUST TRANSFER; IT NEVER SAID WHEN TO BEGIN. Every clause of §H.8 costs context to satisfy — the bridge written, the bank built AND listed, the register rebuilt and its count read, both gates run, the certificate printed with its evidence. A session reaching exhaustion before beginning has no budget to produce any of them, so it hands off without a certificate, and §H.8 says that is not a handoff. THE RESERVE IS PART OF THE PROTOCOL, NOT SLACK IN IT.** *The estimate is declared as an estimate — a session has no counter and errs early, because an early handoff costs one bridge that would have been written anyway while a late one loses the record. On the threshold the session stops OPENING work it cannot close: §2.20's Zeno directive extended from a single execution to the session itself.*

**T3 WITHDRAWN — READING IS ON DEMAND, NOT A QUEUE — BUT THE UNREAD INVENTORY STAYS.** *M: reading will be done as necessary.* **THE THREAD IS REMOVED FROM THE BRIDGE'S §4 AND FROM THE RESUMPTION ORDER. THREADS WERE DETECTED BY THE SAME EXPRESSION THAT REQUIRED AN OWNER, so the clause's stated failure mode — a thread with no owner — could not arise: such a thread does not fail the match, it fails to be a thread. §H.8 says each clause must be capable of failing and §4.6 requires that capability before a pass is evidence; C6 had the form of a check without its content. The general form, and it is the same fault as R 1664's silent default: AN INSTRUMENT THAT NARROWS ITS OWN INPUT REPORTS ON WHAT IT ADMITTED, NOT ON WHAT IT WAS ASKED ABOUT.*

**THE ARCHIVES ARE NOT DISJOINT — THE PROBE WAS, AND IT IS R 1671's FAULT COMMITTED ONE ENTRY LATER.** **I reported that `spectra_raw` and `MEASUREMENTS.tsv` share NO species and that 0 of 554 rows could be re-derived. Both statements are FALSE.

The Method 1.6 — Mathematical Compendium-1.md
**Configuration crossings along isoelectronic sequences** are a computed object:
**Berengut et al., arXiv:1204.0603** locate the 6p–5f crossing in the thallium
sequence by Dirac–Fock.

**The node theorem**, **Pauli's exclusion principle** and the **centrifugal term
ℓ(ℓ+1)** are standard and this work introduces none of them.

**Seaton's ratio** δ₂/δ₀ = −ℓ(ℓ+1)/3 is **Seaton's**; *the domain restriction to
p = 0 is this work's.*

**Slater's rules and integrals** are Slater's; *the observation that the count of
discarded exchange integrals equals the count of bracket failures is this work's.*

---

## What this work introduces, in one list

| object | |
|---|---|
| **the corridor** | 106 consistent linear inequalities with node-count coefficients |
| **the nineteen surds** | the complete set of endpoints across the table |
| **a_cross = (√(n−1)+√(n−4))/3** | closed form for the ns/(n−1)d family |
| **the staircase algebra** | ⌊s/2⌋ ≤ d ≤ s + ⌊s/3⌋, read out of a closed index |
| **the sequence-index fix** | rank parity is not a free coordinate |
| **the selection-rule falsification** | the corridor is forced, the path is not |
| **the necessity of state** | 104 of 106 steps ambiguous without memory |
| **the observability boundary** | closure enumerates; observation values |
| **the singleton-output rule** | an index is closed when its reading is unique |
| **the domain prohibition** | no parameter of this work is universal, so no pooled fit across regions is admissible |
| **the limit** | Λ_spectra closes at the last available species; E = 11, all named |
| **rival = donor iff not full** | the twelve anomalous steps, from Pauli alone |

# The Löwdin indexes — Λ_law and Λ_const

*Owed since register 1296; written at register 1571. Nothing here answers
Löwdin's challenge — the amplitude law remains three fitted numbers.*

## Λ_law — seven laws on (law, carrier). E = 0.

An arbitrary ordering gave E = 7. Across all 7! x 4! = **120,960 orderings** the
defect runs 0 to 21, and **288 reach zero.**

**The closing carrier order is u < p < l - l_core < Z - T**, monotone in **how
LOCAL the variable is**: u is the whole atom, p counts one l's shells,
l - l_core compares two angular momenta, Z - T is one distance to one threshold.
Two laws sit on u, three on p, one on each of the others.

The held cells form a **staircase**, which by `A.staircls` is exactly the
condition for E(R) = 0.

**What only this index contributes: THE CARRIER.** Fitting a law in the wrong
carrier is what took the l-spread from a spurious r2 of 0.868 to a real 0.356.

## Lambda_const — fourteen constants on (role, carrier). E = 0 at 2 of 576.

Role order **exponent < centre < width < scale**. Standing: three fitted, six
measured, five derived or attributed.

**Every CENTRE is a small integer or half-integer** - 2 for the free shells, 2
for the gate, -1.5 for the switch, 2.5 for the l-validity, u0 = 4. **No SCALE
is.** The role axis orders by how much physics a number has absorbed.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
Only 16 series of 486 contain a bracketed member and only 12 have their asymptote on one. I measured Na I, found 8 of 18 and 20 of 36, and wrote the ratio as a property of the store. THAT IS THE PER-ELEMENT-TO-UNIVERSAL FAULT M HAS CORRECTED REPEATEDLY, committed here against my own data while the whole-archive count was one loop away.* **CONSEQUENCE, AND IT FAVOURS M'S RULING: the asymptotic perspective is NOT generally resting on interpolated values. The bracket flag stays as an evidence grade — it is load-bearing for sodium and idle elsewhere, which is what a grade should look like.** *WHAT REMAINS OPEN, stated as a bound: 68 series recovered no members and 128 recovered a count that disagrees with the store. Neither is diagnosed. `store_gen.py` inherits the LIMIT ASSIGNMENT from the store, so it closes the VALUE derivation and not the SERIES construction; C3 coverage of the latter is still open and T6's mechanics are half-built, not built.*

### 1676

**HANDOFF 1.7.3 WRITTEN — AND THE PRACTICE CLAUSES PUT IN THE BRIDGE'S FIRST LINE, NOT ITS LAST.** *`BRIDGE-1_7_3-to-next.md` built to §H.2's eight sections. DIGEST corrected on the point it got wrong: A CELL'S MEMBERS ARE ITS ROWS, and the `members` column is a COUNT of levels, not the levels — which is what made the first session read the collapse as irreversible. Two navigational facts written in because they cost this session a false negative and a wrong claim: `spectra_raw` CONTAINS A DIRECTORY, and M's T6 ruling that the store is authoritative with all three perspectives carried per cell.* **T9 OPENED AND MADE FIRST IN THE RESUMPTION ORDER: 68 series recovered no members and 128 recovered a count disagreeing with the store. 26% unexplained is not a residue, it is an unread finding, and calling it a residue would be the aesthetic deletion M refused at R 1662 wearing a different coat.** *T7's elaboration is recorded as OWED AND UNDELIVERED rather than quietly dropped — M asked for it, the session spent its budget elsewhere, and §H.0's lossy half-state is exactly what an unmarked omission would create.*

### 1677

**T9 DIAGNOSED: THE RESIDUE WAS THE GENERATOR READING ONE LANGUAGE, AND THE THREE NAMED CAUSES ARE ALL REFUSED.** *The bridge named three candidates — term-string variants, J-splitting conventions, and the staging's own n-range cuts. Each was computed and each is a bound (P8/§2.15): the store's own n_lo..n_hi window fixes 7 of 128; parity-only term variants account for 6 of 68; J-splitting is never reached, because the TERMS match and it is the CONFIG that fails.* **AND THE RESIDUE IS LARGER THAN THE BRIDGE STATES. `store_gen.py` dropped the 68 before writing, so they never appeared in MEASUREMENTS-DERIVED.tsv to be counted: 68 + 358 + 128 = 554, and the unexplained share against the SOURCE is 35%, not the 26% computed against the output. A residue measured against a file the fault has already filtered is measured against the fault.** *The true cause, in two parts.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
**

### 1348

**OCCUPANCY ENTERS THROUGH PAULI, AND ONLY THROUGH PAULI.** *The scatter in a within a subshell, with the occupancy fraction q/2(2ℓ+1) inside the radicand against without it:* **3p 0.187 → 0.041 · 4p 0.119 → 0.028 · 5p 0.088 → 0.018 · 6p 0.059 → 0.021 · 5d 0.086 → 0.047. All five improve.** *And the RAW occupancy makes every one worse — 0.211 to 0.407, three to five times worse than doing nothing.* **So the law needs no new coordinate: 2(2ℓ+1) was already the admissibility bound and it belongs in the radicand too. One Pauli quantity, two appearances, and the radicand becomes the count of states below — complete lower shells plus the fraction of the current one filled.**

### 1349

**AND THE TWO REMAINING OBJECTIONS WERE MINE, NOT THE WORK'S.** *I held that the solution fails Löwdin because it does not derive n+ℓ, and because it presupposes orbitals the many-electron Hamiltonian does not contain.* **Both dissolve on results already proved. Register 1307: the observed opening sequence inverts Madelung at 5d/4f and 6d/5f, so deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at La and Ac.** *And register 1327: an index closes when its cells are enumerable, and what it cannot supply is what requires an operator. **(n, ℓ) are the enumeration — the labels of the state space, not an approximation to Ψ.** Asking the equation to hand over orbitals is asking the state to hand over its own labels, which is the category error the method exists to prevent.*

### 1350

**THE LÖWDIN SOLUTION, FINISHED FORM.** *ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√(n−ℓ−1 + q/2(2ℓ+1)); the incoming electron takes the subshell of least ν among those with q < 2(2ℓ+1).* **The corridor L(Z) < a < U(Z) with L,U = Δn(√p_g + √p_r)/(p_g − p_r): 106 of 106 non-empty, nineteen surds, no measurement. a is carried and resets eighteen times, never mid-subshell. Its entry point is t(ℓ) = √(ℓ(ℓ+1)/2) — measured 1.028 at p on four subshells, 1.785 at d on two, ratio √3 to 0.19% — fixed by the single-state ionisation energy.** *Provenance: n−ℓ−1 the node theorem · 2(2ℓ+1) antisymmetry · ℓ(ℓ+1) the centrifugal term from the angular separation · E = ⟨Ψ|Ĥ|Ψ⟩ the observation that fixes what the ordering bounds · the endpoints arithmetic on these.* **No parameter is fitted. Exceptionless on 106 elements including every aufbau anomaly, and right where n+ℓ is wrong. f is outside the domain and the law says so: p = 0 is the node floor, so L = −∞ at every f opening.** WARNING: *'THE LÖWDIN SOLUTION, FINISHED FORM' is withdrawn at register 1460. The form is not the solution and is retained as a form. 'No parameter is fitted' is qualified by R 1445: the 99 of 106 was FITTED — a was placed using each step's own corridor, which is built from the observed entrant — and held out the score is 90 against a null of 96. 'Exceptionless on 106 elements' holds only in that fitted sense.*

### 1351

**MARKED FOR THE ARTEFACT PASS — WHAT EACH ONE NOW OWES.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
That is why E did not move, and the register can now say so from the law rather than from the computation agreeing. And Theorem 10.1 makes the four earlier failures structural rather than unlucky: ADJUNCTION NEVER REPAIRS — a non-closed set cannot be closed by adjoining ANY function of its coordinates, tested on seven including the identity. R 1581, 1599, 1602 and 1608 were not four attempts that happened to fail. They were four attempts at an operation the book proves cannot work.** *THREE FURTHER THINGS THAT BEAR DIRECTLY ON THE INDEX. (i) E3's criterion is that admissibility belongs to the PAIR (h, q) and that only the join can break a bound — meets never do — so Λ_spectra's two rules are safe by inspection exactly as Λ's seven are: each reads one coordinate over a chain, and NONE SUMS. (ii) §17.4's repair is the one we may need later: a sum bound cannot be imposed but a sum can be INDEXED, at the price of making comparable some pairs that were incomparable. (iii) §18.6 says the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), so Λ_spectra at E = 0 can propose nothing — and the place prediction actually lives is the VALUE, not the cell. Which is exactly what the Ga I finding of R 1655 was about: the cell is indexed and settled, and the single delta stored in it is a choice of statistic over a channel that drifts by 0.19.* **AND THE BOOK'S CENTRAL THEOREM HAS OWNERS, WHICH IT SAYS ITSELF: E(X) = 0 IS BERGMAN'S DOUBLE-PROJECTION THEOREM VIA BAKER-PIXLEY 1975, THE CONSTRAINT CLASS IS DEVILLE-BARTAK-VAN HENTENRYCK'S STAIRCASE, AND GLOBAL CONSISTENCY IS MONTANARI AND DECHTER. The book prints its own precedence rather than defending priority, which is the practice this project keeps asking of everything else.** *The read is bounded and its bound is stated: Part II, Chapters 15, 16 and 19, Parts IV through VII with the Löwdin challenge in them, every appendix, and the bodies of all four compendia — about 150,000 words — remain unread. DIGEST.md names them so the gap cannot close over quietly.*

### 1659

**§H — THE HANDOFF PROTOCOL, ADOPTED, WITH A CERTIFICATE THAT CAN FAIL.** *M: prepare everything for a handoff to The Method 1.7.2, and write a protocol that can be referenced, because this need is becoming more common as the work expands. Both done, and the protocol is written to the same standard the book demands of everything else — runnable rather than agreed with.* **THE PROTOCOL NAMES WHAT ACTUALLY GETS LOST, WHICH IS NOT FILES. Files survive a container death; §H.0 states that what dies is WHY — which thread was open, which decision was M's and unmade, which number is a choice wearing the appearance of a measurement. So §H.1 requires four things to travel and calls three of four the dangerous case because it looks like a handoff: the work (the bank), the record (the register), the orientation (DIGEST.md), and the state (the bridge).

import json as _json
_T=_json.load(open("eps0a_table.json")); _xm=np.array([(1-z)**(1/3) for z in _T["zeta"]]); _e0=np.array(_T["eps0a_Ha"])
_o=np.argsort(_xm); _xm=_xm[_o]; _e0=_e0[_o]
E0B=np.log(2)/6-3*1.2020569031595942/(4*np.pi**2)
LAM1=os.environ.get("LAM1","0")=="1"
from lam1_zeta import lam1 as _lam1
from cellcut import SUBCELL as _SUBCELL, frac_neg as _frac_neg
def _cL(z):
    xp,xm=(1+z)**(1/3),(1-z)**(1/3); chi=xp+xm
    with np.errstate(divide='ignore',invalid='ignore'):
        t=xm**3*np.log(np.where(xm>0,xm,1.0))
    return (1/np.pi**2)*((1-np.log(2))+xp*xm/2*chi-np.log(chi)+0.5*(xp**3*np.log(xp)+t))
def _lam0(z): return _cL(z)/2
def _e0a(z): return np.interp((1-z)**(1/3),_xm,_e0)
def v_gbz(nu,nd):
    """pointwise GB high-density eps_c(r_s,zeta); returns (v_up, v_dn), zero where eps>=0."""
    n=nu+nd; n=np.maximum(n,1e-30); z=np.clip((nu-nd)/n,0.0,1.0)
    rs=(3.0/(4*np.pi*n))**(1.0/3.0); L=np.log(rs)
    lam=_lam0(z); e0=_e0a(z); l1=(_lam1(z) if LAM1 else 0.0)
    eps=lam*L+e0+E0B+l1*rs*L
    h=1e-4; zp=np.clip(z+h,0,1); zm=np.clip(z-h,0,1)
    f=lambda zz: _lam0(zz)*L+_e0a(zz)+((_lam1(zz)*rs*L) if LAM1 else 0.0)
    deps_dz=(f(zp)-f(zm))/(zp-zm+1e-300)
    base=eps-lam/3.0-l1*rs*(L+1.0)/3.0        # -(r_s/3) d eps/d r_s
    vu=base+(1-z)*deps_dz; vd=base-(1+z)*deps_dz
    if _SUBCELL:                                   # s28 ruling D: finite-volume in-cell fraction of eps<0 (cellcut.py)
        w=_frac_neg(eps); return vu*w, vd*w

I'm trying to recall the exact Onsager–Mittag-Stephen second-order exchange constant for the unpolarized electron gas, comparing it against the Gell-Mann–Brueckner correlation energy formula in Rydbergs.  After checking the coefficients, I find ε_b = (ln2)/3 − 3ζ(3)/(2π²) Ry ≈ 0.04836 Ry, which equals 0.02418 Ha.

Now I need to extend this to the spin-polarized case. For the fully polarized (ferromagnetic) gas, second-order exchange only pairs same-spin electrons, and I recall from Loos & Gill's work that the polarized constant scales by a factor involving 2^(1/3).

Since the second-order exchange energy per particle of a single species is density-independent, comparing the polarized gas (N electrons, one species) to the unpolarized gas (two species of N/2 each) gives the same total contribution either way — suggesting ε_b might actually be spin-polarization independent, though I should double check this conclusion.

I'm now recalling that this matches Loos & Gill's Phys. Rev. B 84, 033103 (2011) result, which states the second-order exchange energy doesn't depend on ζ — consistent with other references like Gori-Giorgi & Perdew noting ε_b is identical for the unpolarized and fully polarized gas.

I'm trying to verify this through the scaling argument directly: the second-order exchange diagram only involves same-spin electron pairs scattering within the Fermi sphere, and in Rydberg units it reduces to a dimensionless integral with no explicit density scale, which is why it should be independent of r_s at this order. I'm working through the momentum-space structure of the diagram—two same-spin electrons scattering via Coulomb matrix elements with energy denominators set by kinetic energy differences—to confirm this scaling holds.

This confirms the per-particle exchange energy is exactly ζ-independent, so the derivation resolves that part cleanly rather than needing a numerical run. Still, following the protocol, I should state a prediction before doing any computational check — perhaps verifying the second-order exchange integral numerically for a simple case to confirm the analytic result.

Rather than running an expensive multi-dimensional integral, I could instead cross-check against the literature (Loos & Gill 2011) via a quick search, then write the prediction file followed by the finding file. I'm also considering whether the polarized-gas correlation energy data (PW92, Hoffman's eps0a_table) could let me back out the missing piece by comparing known tabulated values.…

content.title: Analytic structure and asymptotic analysis of screened second-order exchange in the uniform electron gas
content.text: Using the linearity of the reduced functional in the screened line, we replace the bare interaction by the physical static RPA (Lindhard) screening, so that the density enters only through the Thomas-Fermi scale rather than an assumed map, and its dependence is set by the endpoints of a single geometric kernel with exponents fixed by the diagram. We prove that this kernel is even and that its quadratic coefficient vanishes identically, so the high-density expansion contains no half-integer power; this justifies the integerpower-times-logarithm form used in recent numerical work and identifies a half-integer term there as an interpolation artifact. The construction extends to arbitrary spin polarization, the bare diagram being polarization-independent, and a dynamical adiabatic-connection evaluation normalized only to that limit reproduces the numerically evaluated kite for both the unpolarized and fully polarized gas, including the low-density sign change.

The final decades of the twentieth century witnessed a major revolution in solid-state and molecular physics, as the introduction of sophisticated exchange-correlation models<sup>1</sup> propelled density-functional theory (DFT) from qualitative to quantitative usefulness. In principle, the foundation of DFT is the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem<sup>2</sup> but, in practice, it is usually the supposed similarity between the electron density in a real system and the electron density in the hypothetical uniform electron gas (UEG).<sup>3</sup>

The three-dimensional UEG is characterized by a density $\rho = \rho_{\uparrow} + \rho_{\downarrow}$ , where $\rho_{\uparrow}$ and $\rho_{\downarrow}$ is the (uniform) density of the spin-up and spin-down electrons, respectively. In order to guarantee its stability, the electrons are assumed to be embedded in a uniform background of positive charge.

In 1965, Kohn and Sham<sup>4</sup> showed that the knowledge of a analytical parametrization of the UEG correlation energy allows one to perform approximate calculations for atoms, molecules and solids. This led to the development of various spin-density correlation functionals (VWN,<sup>5</sup> PZ,<sup>6</sup> PW92,<sup>7</sup> etc.), all of which require information on the high- and low-density regimes of the spin-polarized UEG, and are parametrized using results from near-exact Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations.<sup>8–15</sup>

However, inspired by Wigner's seminal work, <sup>16</sup> Sun, Perdew and Seidl have recently shown that the correlation energy of the UEG can be estimated accurately without any QMC input. <sup>17</sup> They used a "density-parameter interpolation" (DPI) between the (near-)exact high- and low-density regimes, which precisely reproduces the first few coefficients of the high- and low-density energy expansions. <sup>18</sup> Knowledge of these coefficients, of course, is essential for such interpolations and is the motivation for the present work.

The high-density expansion of the correlation energy per electron (or reduced energy) of the UEG is $^{16,17,19-28}$ 

$$E_c(r_s,\zeta) = \lambda_0(\zeta) \ln r_s + \varepsilon_0(\zeta) + \lambda_1(\zeta) r_s \ln r_s + O(r_s),$$
 (1)

where $r_s = (4\pi\rho/3)^{-1/3}$ is the so-called Seitz radius, and $\zeta = (\rho_{\uparrow} - \rho_{\downarrow})/\rho$ is the relative spin polarization. It is clear that $\lambda_0(\zeta)$ , $\varepsilon_0(\zeta)$ , $\lambda_1(\zeta)$ , ... must be even functions. We use atomic units throughout.

The coefficient $\lambda_1(\zeta)$ can be written similarly<sup>24</sup> as

$$\lambda_1(\zeta) = \lambda_1^{\mathbf{a}}(\zeta) + \lambda_1^{\mathbf{b}}(\zeta), \tag{7}$$

where

$$\lambda_1^{\mathbf{a}}(\zeta) = -\frac{3\alpha}{8\pi^5} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal{R}_1^{\mathbf{a}}(u,\zeta) \, du, \tag{8}$$

$$\lambda_1^{\rm b}(\zeta) = \frac{3\alpha}{16\pi^4} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal{R}_1^{\rm b}(u,\zeta) \, du \tag{9}$$

are the RPA and second-order exchange contributions and $\alpha=\left(9\pi/4\right)^{-1/3}$ . The integrand functions are<sup>7,17</sup>

$$\mathcal{R}_{1}^{a}(u,\zeta) = R_{0}(u,\zeta)^{2} R_{1}(u,\zeta), \tag{10}$$

$$\mathcal{R}_1^{\mathbf{b}}(u,\zeta) = R_0(u,\zeta)R_2(iu,\zeta),\tag{11}$$

$$R_1(u,\zeta) = k_{\downarrow}^{-1} R_1 \left(\frac{u}{k_{\downarrow}}\right) + k_{\uparrow}^{-1} R_1 \left(\frac{u}{k_{\uparrow}}\right), \qquad (12)$$

$$R_2(iu,\zeta) = R_2\left(i\frac{u}{k_\perp}\right) + R_2\left(i\frac{u}{k_\uparrow}\right),$$
 (13)

$$R_1(u) = -\frac{\pi}{3(1+u^2)^2},\tag{14}$$

$$R_2(iu) = 4\frac{(1+3u^2) - u(2+3u^2)\arctan u}{1+u^2}.$$
 (15)

Carr and Maradudin gave an estimate<sup>24</sup> of $\lambda_1(0)$ and this was later refined by Perdew and coworkers.<sup>7,17</sup>

However, we have found that the integrals in Eqs. 8 and 9 can be evaluated exactly by computer software, <sup>30</sup> giving the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic values in Table I and the spin-scaling functions

$$\Lambda_{1}^{a}(\zeta) = \frac{3}{\pi^{2} - 6} \left\{ \left( \frac{\pi^{2}}{6} + \frac{1}{4} \right) (k_{\downarrow}^{2} + k_{\uparrow}^{2}) - \frac{3}{2} k_{\downarrow} k_{\uparrow} - \frac{k_{\downarrow}^{2} + k_{\uparrow}^{2}}{k_{\downarrow}^{2} - k_{\uparrow}^{2}} k_{\downarrow} k_{\uparrow} \ln \left( \frac{k_{\downarrow}}{k_{\uparrow}} \right) - \frac{k_{\downarrow}^{2} - k_{\uparrow}^{2}}{2} \left[ \operatorname{Li}_{2} \left( \frac{k_{\downarrow} - k_{\uparrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) - \operatorname{Li}_{2} \left( \frac{k_{\uparrow} - k_{\downarrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) \right] \right\}, (16)$$

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>b</sup> Results taken from Ref. 17 using the DPI (density-parameter interpolation) formula with $\lambda_1(1) = 0.003125$ .

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>c</sup> Results from the present work using the DPI formula with $\lambda_1(1) = 0.004792$ .

$$\Lambda_{1}^{b}(\zeta) = \frac{3}{\pi^{2} - 12 \ln 2} \left\{ \frac{\pi^{2}}{6} (k_{\downarrow}^{2} + k_{\uparrow}^{2}) + (1 - \ln 2)(k_{\downarrow} - k_{\uparrow})^{2} - \frac{k_{\downarrow}^{2}}{2} \operatorname{Li}_{2} \left( \frac{k_{\downarrow} - k_{\uparrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) - \frac{k_{\uparrow}^{2}}{2} \operatorname{Li}_{2} \left( \frac{k_{\uparrow} - k_{\downarrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) + \frac{1}{k_{\downarrow} k_{\uparrow}} \left[ k_{\downarrow}^{4} \ln \left( \frac{k_{\downarrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) + k_{\downarrow}^{2} k_{\uparrow}^{2} \ln \left( \frac{k_{\downarrow} k_{\uparrow}}{(k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow})^{2}} \right) + k_{\uparrow}^{4} \ln \left( \frac{k_{\uparrow}}{k_{\downarrow} + k_{\uparrow}} \right) \right] \right\}, (17)$$

where $Li_2$ is the dilogarithm function.<sup>29</sup>

The spin-scalings $\Lambda_0(\zeta)$ , $\Upsilon_0^a(\zeta)$ , $\Upsilon_0^b(\zeta)$ , $\Lambda_1^a(\zeta)$ and $\Lambda_1^b(\zeta)$ are shown in Fig. 1, highlighting the Hoffmann minimum<sup>28</sup> in $\Upsilon_0^a(\zeta)$ near $\zeta = 0.9956$ and revealing a similar minimum in $\Lambda_1^a(\zeta)$ near $\zeta = 0.9960$ . Such minima seem to be ubiquitous in RPA coefficients.

The data in Table I yield the exact values

$$\lambda_1(0) = \frac{\alpha}{4\pi^3} \left( \frac{7\pi^2}{6} - 12 \ln 2 - 1 \right)$$

$$= 0.00922921 \dots, \qquad (18)$$

$$\lambda_1(1) = 2^{-4/3} \frac{\alpha}{4\pi^3} \left( \frac{13\pi^2}{12} - 12 \ln 2 + \frac{1}{2} \right)$$

$$= 0.00479225 \dots, \qquad (19)$$

and it is revealing to compare these with recent numerical calculations. The estimate $\lambda_1(0) \approx 0.0092292$ by Sun *et al.*<sup>17</sup> agrees perfectly with Eq. (18) but their estimate $\lambda_1(1) \approx 0.003125$ is strikingly different from Eq. (19). How can this discrepancy be explained?

Following Gell-Mann and Brueckner, <sup>22</sup> and Ueda, <sup>31</sup> Misawa argued <sup>25</sup> that the $\zeta=0$ and $\zeta=1$ limits of the RPA and exchange contributions to the correlation energy are related by

$$E_{\rm c}^{\rm a}(r_s,1) = \frac{1}{2} E_{\rm c}^{\rm a}(2^{-4/3}r_s,0),$$
 (20)

$$E_{\rm c}^{\rm b}(r_s, 1) = E_{\rm c}^{\rm b}(2^{-4/3}r_s, 0),$$
 (21)

and, from these relations, Perdew and Wang inferred<sup>7</sup>

$$\lambda_1^{\mathbf{a}}(1) = 2^{-7/3} \lambda_1^{\mathbf{a}}(0), \tag{22}$$

$$\lambda_1^{\mathbf{b}}(1) = 2^{-4/3} \lambda_1^{\mathbf{b}}(0). \tag{23}$$

These are also obtained if the $\zeta \to 1$ limit of the integrands in Eqs. 8 and 9 is taken before integrating over u.

Numerical evaluations of Eq. (9) and analytical results from Eq. (17) confirm that Eq. (23) is correct. However, numerical evaluations of Eq. 8 and analytical results from Eq. (16) agree that Eq. (22) is wrong and that, in fact,

$$\lambda_1^{\rm a}(1) = 2^{-7/3} \lambda_1^{\rm a}(0) \times \frac{\pi^2 + 6}{\pi^2 - 6}.$$
 (24)

The error in Eq. (22) arises from the non-commutativity of the $\zeta \to 1$ limit and the u integration, which is due to the non-uniform convergence of $\mathcal{R}_1^a(u,\zeta)$ .

To show this particular point, let us define

$$\Delta \lambda_1^{\rm a}(\zeta) = -\frac{3\alpha}{8\pi^5} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\rm a}(u,\zeta) \, du, \tag{25}$$

$$\Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\mathrm{a}}(u,\zeta) = \frac{k_{\uparrow}^2}{k_{\downarrow}} R_0 \left(\frac{u}{k_{\uparrow}}\right)^2 R_1 \left(\frac{u}{k_{\downarrow}}\right). \tag{26}$$

It can be easily shown that it is not possible to find a function D(u), which is integrable with respect to u and dominates $\Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\rm a}(u,\zeta)$ , i.e. $\forall (u,\zeta), |\Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\rm a}(u,\zeta)| \leq D(u)$ . Thus, according to the dominated convergence theorem, one cannot show that limit and integration can be interchanged, and

$$\lim_{\zeta \to 1} \Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\mathbf{a}}(u,\zeta) = 0, \qquad \qquad \Delta \lambda_1^{\mathbf{a}}(1) = 0. \tag{27}$$

However, substituting $t = u/k_{\downarrow}$ in Eqs. (25) and (26), one immediately finds a function D(t), which is integrable with respect to t and dominates $\Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\rm a}(t,\zeta)$ . This ensures the possibility of interchanging limit and integration. It yields

$$\lim_{\zeta \to 1} \Delta \mathcal{R}_1^{\mathbf{a}}(t,\zeta) = -\frac{2^{2/3}\pi}{3(1+t^2)^2},\tag{28}$$

$$\Delta \lambda_1^{\rm a}(1) = \frac{3\alpha}{8\pi^5} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{2^{2/3}\pi}{3(1+t^2)^2} dt$$

$$= 2^{-1/3} \frac{\alpha}{8\pi^3} = 0.00166727,$$
(29)

which is exactly the difference between the two values of $\lambda_1^a(1)$ .

The effect of the coefficient $\lambda_1(1)$ on the reduced correlation energy of the ferromagnetic state has been studied by varying its value in the DPI formula proposed by Sun et al. in Ref. 17. The results have been compared with the benchmark QMC calculations of Ceperley and Alder.<sup>8</sup> As shown in Table II, the new value of $\lambda_1(1)$ derived in the present study systematically improves the accuracy of the DPI correlation energy, especially for small $r_s$ .

In some cases, $^{27,32}$ it is of interest to resolve $\lambda_1(\zeta)$ into contributions due to $\uparrow \uparrow$ , $\downarrow \downarrow$ and $\uparrow \downarrow$ electron pairs, such as

$$\lambda_1^{i}(\zeta) = \lambda_1^{i,\uparrow\uparrow}(\zeta) + \lambda_1^{i,\downarrow\downarrow}(\zeta) + \lambda_1^{i,\uparrow\downarrow}(\zeta), \qquad (30)$$

$$\Lambda_1^{i,\sigma\sigma'}(\zeta) = \frac{\lambda_1^{i,\sigma\sigma'}(\zeta)}{\lambda_1^i(\zeta)},\tag{31}$$

where i = a or b, and $\sigma \sigma' = \uparrow \uparrow$ , $\downarrow \downarrow$ or $\uparrow \downarrow$ . Using (16) and

![](_page_3_Figure_1.jpeg)

FIG. 2. Spin-resolution of $\Lambda_1^{a,\sigma\sigma'}(\zeta)$ , $\Lambda_1^{b,\sigma\sigma'}(\zeta)$ and $\lambda_1^{\sigma\sigma'}(\zeta)$ as functions of $\zeta$ .

(17), we find

$$\Lambda_1^{a,\uparrow\uparrow}(\zeta) = \frac{1}{8} \frac{\pi^2 + 6}{\pi^2 - 6} \frac{(1+\zeta)^{2/3}}{\Lambda_1^a(\zeta)},\tag{32}$$

$$\Lambda_1^{\mathrm{b},\uparrow\uparrow}(\zeta) = \frac{1}{4} \frac{(1+\zeta)^{2/3}}{\Lambda_1^{\mathrm{b}}(\zeta)}.$$
 (33)

The remaining contributions can be obtained using the relations

$$\Lambda_1^{i,\downarrow\downarrow}(\zeta) = \Lambda_1^{i,\uparrow\uparrow}(-\zeta),\tag{34}$$

$$\Lambda_1^{i,\uparrow\downarrow}(\zeta) = 1 - \Lambda_1^{i,\uparrow\uparrow}(\zeta) - \Lambda_1^{i,\downarrow\downarrow}(\zeta), \tag{35}$$

and are represented in Fig. 2.

In conclusion, we have found a closed-form expression for the coefficient $\lambda_1(\zeta)$ of the $r_s \ln r_s$ term in Eq. (1). It is valid for any value of $\zeta$ and, in particular, for the paramagnetic ( $\zeta = 0$ ) and ferromagnetic ( $\zeta = 1$ ) limits.

This reveals that an earlier derivation of the ferromagnetic limit $\lambda_1(1)$ was incorrect because of an inadmissible interchange of a limit and an integral. The present result has no direct impact on the quantum phase diagram of the UEG, because the effect of the coefficient $\lambda_1(\zeta)$ is more pronounced in the high-density limit $(0 < r_s \lesssim 2)$ , where the paramagnetic fluid is significantly more stable than the ferromagnetic one.<sup>8</sup> Preliminary results on higher-order coefficients reveal that they behave similarly, and special care has to be taken in future studies. We believe that these new results will be useful in the future development of exchange-correlation functionals within DFT.

I've confirmed from Table I that ε_0^b(ζ) equals ln2/6 − 3ζ(3)/(4π²) at both ζ=0 and ζ=1, with Υ_0^b=1, meaning E0B(ζ) equals E0B exactly — this resolves point (1)(i) using OMS 1966 for the value and Loos-Gill 2011 Table I for the ζ-independence, plus the scaling argument. But this implies Cs still gets cut 31% at ζ~1 since E0B doesn't depend on ζ, which I need to reconcile.

Actually I'm realizing there's a deeper inconsistency: combining the fully resummed ring diagrams with a bare second-order exchange constant is mismatched, since at large r_s the bare SOX term should be screened and suppressed rather than staying constant, while the ring sum is valid at all orders — so the "ring + bare E0B" construction breaks down at low density in the same way a truncated expansion would, and I should check whether the 2026 arXiv paper on screened second-order exchange addresses this polarization-independent bare term issue.

Given the derivation shows E0B(ζ) is constant, the earlier concern about the R/Z comparison being unfair on Cs dissolves — the cut is simply an inherent feature of form R, not an artifact. I'll flag the screened-SOX idea as a candidate for M's ruling without pursuing it further, then move to writing the prediction file (PREDICTION-E0B-SESSION-31.md) stating PE1: E0B(ζ) is ζ-independent, before running the actual check.…

"""corr_ring.py -- s30 candidate C: eps_c^R(nu,nd) = eps_r(r_s,zeta)/2 + E0B  [Ha] from ring_table.json; v^R = d(n eps)/dn (spin-resolved) by table gradients.
Same interface as t7c_cuaudit.v_gbz / hfc2.eps_c so it can be patched in: T.v_gbz = v_R; H.eps_c = eps_R. Small-r_s: below table, chain form (lam0 ln rs+eps0+E0B)."""
import numpy as np, json, t7c_cuaudit as T
_tab=json.load(open('ring_table.json')); RS=np.array(_tab['rs']); ZS=np.array(_tab['z']); LR=np.log(RS)
E=np.array([_tab['eps'][str(i)] for i in range(len(ZS))])/2.0+T.E0B          # (nz, nrs) Ha
dE_dlnrs=np.gradient(E,LR,axis=1); dE_dz=np.gradient(E,ZS,axis=0)
def _interp(A,lr,z):
    iz=np.clip(np.searchsorted(ZS,z)-1,0,len(ZS)-2); tz=(z-ZS[iz])/(ZS[iz+1]-ZS[iz])
    ir=np.clip(np.searchsorted(LR,lr)-1,0,len(LR)-2); tr=(lr-LR[ir])/(LR[ir+1]-LR[ir])
    a=A[iz,ir]*(1-tr)+A[iz,ir+1]*tr; b=A[iz+1,ir]*(1-tr)+A[iz+1,ir+1]*tr
    return a*(1-tz)+b*tz
def _chain(rs,z): return T._lam0(z)*np.log(rs)+T._e0a(z)+T.E0B
def eps_R(nu,nd):
    n=nu+nd; n=np.maximum(n,1e-30); z=np.clip((nu-nd)/n,0.0,1.0); rs=(3.0/(4*np.pi*n))**(1.0/3.0); lr=np.log(rs)
    lo=lr<LR[0]; hi=lr>LR[-1]
    e=_interp(E,np.clip(lr,LR[0],LR[-1]),z)
    e=np.where(lo,_chain(rs,z),e); e=np.where(hi,_interp(E,LR[-1]*np.ones_like(lr),z),e)   # beyond r_s=100: clamp (negligible density)
    return e
def v_R(nu,nd):
    n=nu+nd; n=np.maximum(n,1e-30); z=np.clip((nu-nd)/n,0.0,1.0); rs=(3.0/(4*np.pi*n))**(1.0/3.0); lr=np.log(rs); lrc=np.clip(lr,LR[0],LR[-1])
    eps=eps_R(nu,nd); de_dl=_interp(dE_dlnrs,lrc,z); de_dz=_interp(dE_dz,lrc,z)
    lo=lr<LR[0]
    de_dl=np.where(lo,T._lam0(z),de_dl)
    h=1e-4; de_dz=np.where(lo,(_chain(rs,np.clip(z+h,0,1))-_chain(rs,np.clip(z-h,0,1)))/(np.clip(z+h,0,1)-np.clip(z-h,0,1)+1e-300),de_dz)
    base=eps-de_dl/3.0                              # -(r_s/3) d eps/d r_s = -(1/3) d eps/d ln r_s
    vu=base+(1-z)*de_dz; vd=base-(1+z)*de_dz
    if T._SUBCELL: w=T._frac_neg(eps); return vu*w, vd*w
    ok=eps<0; return np.where(ok,vu,0.0), np.where(ok,vd,0.0)
if __name__=="__main__":
    for rs in (1e-3,1e-2,0.1,1,2,3,5,10):
        n=3/(4*np.pi*rs**3)
        for z in (0.0,1.0):
            print(f"rs {rs} z {z}: R {float(eps_R(n*(1+z)/2*np.ones(1),n*(1-z)/2*np.ones(1))[0]):+.5f}  Z {float(_chain(rs,z)):+.5f} Ha")

I also need to make sure corr_ring's v_R handles NaN masking robustly within the SCF loop, similar to how frachf_ring used it previously.

Now I'm planning the order of prediction files to write: first PREDICTION-E0B with the timing flag and its corresponding FINDING-E0B, closing item (1)(i) and treating (1)(ii) as a no-op since the rows stand unchanged. Then, before running anything, I want to lay out PREDICTION-RZ with specific hypotheses comparing ER vs EZ — that R should deliver deeper shifts than Z on every row with a shift ratio around 1.2-1.5, that this gain ratio should stay fairly uniform across the 3d rows, and that the 4f rows will show distinct behavior under the R form as well.…

content.thinking:
Reassembling the full-chain residuals row by row is messy, so instead I'm focusing on the cleaner differential ΔE = ER − EZ per row to see how form R shifts each row and whether that shift depends on class. I can cross-check against the measured residuals already computed for class rows, and look at the 3d and 4f residual magnitudes under the term-HF-plus-chain correction.

Looking at the chain-side behavior, the LSD chain residuals are uniformly negative while R pushes them more negative still, even as R reduces the positive term-HF residual — so R narrows one side of the bracket while widening the other. Computing the R/Z shift ratios by element, I see they cluster differently by class: roughly 1.11–1.24 for 3d, 1.38–1.43 for the heavier nd≥4 group, and 1.13–1.18 for 4f, with Cs as an outlier at 2.32 — so the ratio clearly isn't uniform across classes, which is worth digging into further.

Let me check the class-row residuals for R versus Z: the Z residuals show a spread of about 0.010 between 3d and nd≥4 elements, while R residuals show a similar spread of roughly 0.009-0.012, so the two don't clearly differentiate on this criterion.

Checking the Sc numbers against FINDING-RING, the residual shift doesn't match the eigenvalue shift I'd expect, so these must be tracking different quantities —…

Dissected residual shifts across element classes and cross-validated findings.

content.thinking:
I'm checking each prediction zone against tolerance: PZ0 and PZ1 hold cleanly, PZ2 holds marginally with Cr at -9%, and PZ3's 4f ratios fall in the same band as 3d, so it holds too, though I'm noting the deeper rows shift by a small residual that needs tracing back through the chain logic.

PZ4 fails outright — Cs comes in at 2.32 against a predicted 2.5-3.0 range, missing by 0.2, and I realize the earlier 2.8 figure was measuring a different quantity entirely. PZ5 holds comfortably since 13-14 of 15 rows fall below the U threshold under R, far more than the 7 under Z. The bigger pattern I'm seeing now is that the R/Z gain ratio splits cleanly by orbital class — nd≥4 at 1.41, 3d at 1.18, 4f at 1.16, ns at 2.32 — which means the truncation isn't uniform at all; it costs the nd≥4 rows a disproportionately larger share than the earlier "uniform gain" framing suggested.

This class split actually tracks r_s: compact 3d/4f orbitals lose less to truncation (1.16-1.18), diffuse nd≥4 orbitals lose more (1.41), and the extended Cs 6s orbital loses the most (2.3) — a monotone ordering by spatial extent, which makes sense since truncation error should scale with orbital size. Now I'm checking whether this same pattern shows up in the residual spread across classes: under Z the gap between 3d and nd≥4 residuals is about 0.010, and I'm working out the equivalent gap under R.

I can frame R's remaining defect as a known literature property (RPA overbinding ~0.035 Ry flat) rather than a validity failure, though that's a judgment call, not the criterion itself—the ruling belongs to M. I should also flag that PZ4 failed with no timing issues, and note that for the 3d/4f rows, R deepens them by 0.006-0.008, pushing the already-negative LSD chain residual further negative.…

Scrutinized prediction zones systematically, uncovered orbital-class truncation patterns.

# COMPARE-RZ — the 15 chain rows under form R (full RPA ring + E0B) vs form Z (truncated GB), SIC_NOCLAMP=1 SUBCELL=1.  s31.
# Files: PREDICTION-RZ (before the run) · t7c_corrz.py (corr='R' hook, s31) · t7c_corrRZ_run.py · t7c_corrz_sc.jsonl (Z, SUBCELL=1) · t7c_corrR.jsonl (R).
# E = entrant TS eigenvalue of the SIC+corr chain (Ha); shift = E - base (base = noclamp SIC chain without correlation, t7c_regen). U,P: the s23 bracket.
EOF
cat /tmp/rz.txt
cat <<'EOF'
## Predictions scored
PZ0 HELD: Z under SUBCELL=1 == s23 Z rows to 0.0001 (La) on all 15 — the s23 Z rows stand as the SUBCELL=1 rows.
PZ1 HELD: R deeper than Z on every row (dR-Z -0.0020 Cr .. -0.0077 Cu; -0.0041 Cs).
PZ2 HELD (marginal): 3d ratio 1.11 (Cr) .. 1.24 (Ti), all within 10 % of Sc 1.22.
PZ3 HELD: 4f ratio 1.13-1.18, the SAME band as 3d (1.16 vs 1.18 mean); 4f rows deepen by 0.0055-0.0071 — form R does NOT close the 4f +0.09.
PZ4 FAILED: Cs ratio 2.32 (predicted 2.5-3.0 from frachf_ring's delivered 0.45/0.16 = 2.8; that was the sc-path DEc, a different object).
PZ5 HELD: rows below U — Z 7/15 (Fe Ni Cu Dy Er Tm Yb), R 14/15 (all but Cr).
## What the run says (before the criterion)
(1) The R/Z gain in the eigenvalue shift is CLASS-RESOLVED and ORDERED BY DIFFUSENESS: 3d 1.18 ~ 4f 1.16 < nd>=4 1.41 < 6s 2.32. FINDING-RING's "uniform gain"
    was in units of required correlation (+0.22..0.29); in units of the row's own Z correlation the truncation costs the diffuse rows more — the truncation
    error grows with r_s (Nozieres-Pines validity r_s <~ 1), and the compact 3d/4f shells sit at one value. This is a FORM property, monotone in r_s.
(2) Self-consistency across paths: Sc 1.22 / Y 1.38 here vs frachf_ring's 1.24 / 1.38 (sc path). The two chain routes agree on the R/Z gain to 0.02.
(3) The two-sided bracket (s27): term-HF+chain-corr side POSITIVE (3d +0.02..+0.07, 4f +0.09..+0.10), LSD chain side NEGATIVE. R deepens every row by
    0.002-0.008: it NARROWS the term-HF side by that amount and WIDENS the LSD side by the same amount. Neither side closes; the 4f object survives at ~+0.08-0.09.
## The pre-stated criterion (class-spread of the residual against RECALLED IEs), on the rows where a chain residual is on record (FINDING-RING, class rows)
    resid_Z: Sc -0.0022 · Y -0.0131 · La -0.0103 · Lu -0.0123 · Cs -0.0130  -> 3d-vs-nd>=4 gap ~0.010, one sign.
    resid_R: Sc -0.0040 · Y +0.0054 · La +0.0019 · Lu +0.0043 · Cs +0.0086  -> gap ~0.008, SIGN FLIPS across the class.
    On the criterion the forms differ by ~0.002 in class-spread: NOT DECISIVE. The d-row object (~0.005-0.008, non-local, nd>=4) is present under both, as
    FINDING-RING stated. 3d/4f residuals under R are not on record as full-chain rows here (the term assembly is not re-run in s31; PZ3 bounds the change).
## Statement (not a ruling)
    R: derived, valid at all r_s, defect = known RPA overbinding (~0.035 Ry, nearly flat) + the bare-SOX/ring mismatch at zeta~1 large r_s (Cs).
    Z: derived, valid r_s <~ 1, defect = truncation, r_s-monotone (this run), happens to cancel on Sc.
    The comparison SEPARATES the forms by the r_s-dependence of their defect (Z's is monotone in diffuseness, R's is flat) but NOT by the class-spread
    criterion at the 0.002 level. Which is the chain's correlation is M's ruling. If R: 14/15 rows lie below the s23 U edge (the U/P bracket was built under
    Z and is not a criterion for R). Failed prediction: PZ4. Timing flags: none (PREDICTION-RZ before the hook ran).
Gates for HANDOFF-31: SIC_NOCLAMP=1 SUBCELL=1 FORM=R python3 t7c_corrRZ_run.py 21 39 55 -> must SKIP all; if Sc deleted reprints EF -0.3265 shift -0.0299 (4 s);
    FORM=Z ... 21 -> SKIP; if deleted reprints EF -0.3211. Gate 16 unchanged (-0.5 for corr='Z' and corr='R').
EOF
} > pack31/COMPARE-RZ-SESSION-31.md; cp rt/t7c_corrz.py rt/t7c_corrRZ_run.py rt/t7c_corrz_sc.jsonl rt/t7c_corrR.jsonl pack31/; ls pack31; grep -n "eps(0)\|slope" pack30/FINDING-DROW-P-SESSION-30.md pack30/COMPARE-DROW-SESSION-30.md | head -6 | cut -c1-260

"""frachf_eps0.py -- s31 item (2): Sc eps(f=1e-3) by a run (corr and hf paths) in place of the linear extrapolation eps(0):=2eps(1/4)-eps(1/2).
Writes frachf_eps0.jsonl (side file; frachf.jsonl untouched). usage: python3 frachf_eps0.py Z [F]"""
import sys,os,json,time,numpy as np
os.environ.setdefault("SIC_NOCLAMP","1"); os.environ.setdefault("SUBCELL","1")
import hfc2 as H; from t7c_kernel import C0; from t5_scf import ground_occ; import t7c_cuaudit as T
Z=int(sys.argv[1]); F=float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv)>2 else 1e-3; sys.argv=[sys.argv[0]]
exec(open('frachf.py').read().split('def path')[0].split('import t7c_cuaudit as T')[1])   # HFCf, SH, OUT
OUT="frachf_eps0.jsonl"; done={(d['Z'],d['f']) for d in map(json.loads,open(OUT))} if os.path.exists(OUT) else set()
if (Z,F) in done: print("SKIP",Z,F); sys.exit()
el,sh=SH[Z]; n,l=int(sh[0]),"spdf".index(sh[1]); occ0=ground_occ(Z); t0=time.time(); res={}
for corr in (True,False):
    H.CORR=corr; occ=[(a,b,(F if (a,b)==(n,l) else q)) for a,b,q in occ0]
    h=HFCf(Z,occ,c=C0); h.ent=(n,l); h.f=F; h.frac={(n,l):(0,F)}
    E,Ec,it,eps=h.run2(); res['corr' if corr else 'hf']=dict(E=float(E),Ec=float(Ec),eps=float(eps[(n,l)]),it=it)
FR={d['Z']:d for d in map(json.loads,open('frachf.jsonl'))}[Z]
e=lambda p,f:FR[p][str(f)]['eps']
out=dict(Z=Z,el=el,sh=sh,f=F,run=res)
for p,k in (('corr_path','corr'),('hf_path','hf')):
    e0lin=2*e(p,0.25)-e(p,0.5); e0run=res[k]['eps']
    simp_lin=(e0lin+4*e(p,0.5)+e(p,1.0))/6; simp_run=(e0run+4*e(p,0.5)+e(p,1.0))/6
    D=FR['D_tot_corr'] if k=='corr' else FR['D_HF']
    out[k]=dict(eps0_lin=round(e0lin,6),eps0_run=round(e0run,6),simp_lin=round(simp_lin,6),simp_run=round(simp_run,6),D=D,gap_lin=round(D-simp_lin,6),gap_run=round(D-simp_run,6))
out['sec']=int(time.time()-t0)
open(OUT,'a').write(json.dumps(out)+'\n'); print(json.dumps(out))
EOF

# THE METHOD 1.6 — MATHEMATICAL COMPENDIUM

Generated from `mathreg.py` on 2026-08-12. **248 objects · 17 roots · 246 settled · 2 unfinished.**

**Verification coverage, stated rather than implied.** `mathverify.py` makes **103 assertions naming 46 of these objects** and recomputes each stated value against the register; **no verifier touches the other 167**. Of the check fields, **85 state a finding, 91 repeat the object's own key, 19 name a function, and 18 are empty** — so a check field present is not a verification performed. `check_audit.py` classifies them on any build. Register 849.

Rebuild with `python3 compendium.py > COMPENDIUM.md`. It reads the register, so it cannot
drift from what the book actually holds.

---

# I · THE CYCLE

The whole of this work is one recursion, stated at §14.5.2:

> **X₍ₙ₊₁₎ = ℛ(X_n ∪ Δ_n)**, halting when **Δ_n ⊆ ℛ(X_n)** — when the increment is already implied.

**It has never halted.** Its falsifier is the ratio of closure to seed:

| | |
|---|---|
| closure — objects the register holds | **248** |
| seed — objects nothing derives | **17** |
| ratio | **14.6 : 1** |

**The seed has not moved across every cycle of this project.** If a genuinely new mathematical
object entered that nothing existing derived, it would move — and that is the test.

## The fourteen roots

| object | statement |
|---|---|
| `A.alph` | Â_i(X) = { x_i : x ∈ X } |
| `A.seaton` | delta(n) = (alpha/K(l))(3 - l(l+1)/n^2) for a non-penetrating series, so delta_0 = 3 alpha/K and delta_2 = -l( |
| `B.adm` | r = 2Z²R/(ν³σ) ≥ 5 |
| `B.brk` | T(n) lies between T(n−1) and T(n+1) |
| `B.coll` | an observable ⟨r⟩^a/(ΔE)^b scales as ν^{2a+3b} |
| `B.nuV` | ν_V = (3Z²R/5q)^{1/4} |
| `L.c1` | ℓ ≤ n − 1 |
| `L.c2` | k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1) = 4ℓ+2 |
| `L.c3` | q ≤ k |
| `L.c4` | f ≤ e − 1 |
| `L.c5` | g ≤ 4f+2 |

| `L.c8` | k ≥ 1 (definitional restriction, not a bound) |

| `P.qdt` | the quantum defect measures how far a Rydberg orbital reaches into the ionic core |
| `P.trunc` | truncation removes most channels and degrades those it leaves |

---

# II · THE OPERATORS

Every derivation in the book runs through these. Nine are this work's own.

The Method 1.6 — The Register-1.md
*

### 1374

**THE SPECIES LADDERS ARE SIX, NOT FOUR, AND THE EXTRA TWO ARE ARITHMETIC.** Z = Nₑ + c − 1 is one linear relation on three named quantities; fixing each in turn gives isoelectronic, the walk, ionisation. The nuclide chart carries the exact parallel A = Z + N, and fixing each of its three gives isotopic, isotonic, isobaric. 1356 treated the nuclear direction as one orthogonal ladder; the relation admits three by the same argument, and no collection is needed to enumerate them. **The repair matters structurally: at six ladders, ionisation and isotopic both fix Z, so `fixes` stops individuating the cells** — which is what breaks the vacuity, since at four ladders `fixes` was injective and 0 of 60 comparable arrangements could refuse anything.

### 1375

**A COORDINATE THAT INDIVIDUATES THE CELLS IS A KEY, NOT AN AXIS: THE DUAL OF A.DEFINE.** A.define records that a rung-1 coordinate contributes no envelope — one value, nothing to bound. The other end of the same degeneracy is a coordinate with as many values as there are cells: **it also contributes no envelope**, because every cell is alone in its row and the monotonising ordering always exists. Measured: 4-cell sets on a 4×4×2 grid with axis 0 injective, 0 of 60 reach E > 0; at five cells 20 of 60, at six 51, at seven 59. So injectivity forces closure only while the cell count is small, and the two conditions must be reported together. **E = 0 is informative only where refusal was possible, and that is a property of the arrangement, not of the operator.**

### 1376

content.title: Screened second-order exchange in the uniform electron gas: exact reduction, a single-pole reference model and asymptotic analysis | Cool Papers - Immersive Paper Discovery
content.text:
We derive an exact reduction of the screened second-order exchange (SOSEX) energy in the uniform electron gas to a triple integral for a specific class of single-pole screened interaction. The reduction proceeds by rescaling the frequency variable to factorize the propagator denominators, applying ...

We derive an exact reduction of the screened second-order exchange (SOSEX) energy in the uniform electron gas to a triple integral for a specific class of single-pole screened interaction. The reduction proceeds by rescaling the frequency variable to factorize the propagator denominators, applying a Fourier decomposition to separate the two particle-hole blocks, and finally performing a change of integration variables that brings the geometric structure into a tractable form. 

The reduction to a one-variable integral kernel is possible if and only if the screened interaction belongs to a one-pole class characterized by a single momentum-independent frequency scale~$μ$, which we call the reduction-compatible single-pole (RC-SP) model. The RC-SP model does not approximate plasmon dispersions in real materials, but provides an exactly reducible reference model for analyzing dynamically screened exchange, and gives natural basis elements for approximating more general one-pole screening.

content.title: Two approximate screening functions for the neutral Thomas-Fermi atom
content.text:
# Two approximate screening functions for the neutral Thomas-Fermi atom

Herbert E. Müller http://herbert-mueller.info/

#### Abstract

In the Thomas-Fermi model for the atom or ion, the electric potential $\phi$ and electron density n are both expressed in terms of a screening number $\chi$ and the radius x. The second order differential equation for the screening function $\chi(x)$ cannot be solved in closed form. Two approximate formulas for the screening function of the neutral atom are proposed: the first formula is analytically simple, the second formula has the roles of dependent and independent variable interchanged. Both formulas reproduce the true screening function very accurately.

#### 1 Introduction

In quantum chemistry, electron densities of atoms and molecules are described with the Thomas-Fermi model and refinements thereof. The second order differential equations for the electric potential that come with these models cannot be solved in closed form.

content.title: The self-energy of the uniform electron gas in the second order of   exchange
content.text:
The self-energy of the uniform electron gas in the second order of exchange

# P. Ziesche

Max-Planck-Institut für Physik komplexer Systeme Nöthnitzer Str. 38, D-01187 Dresden, Germany pz@pks.mpg.de

## PACS 71.10.Ca, 05.30.Fk

The on-shell self-energy of the homogeneous electron gas in second order of exchange, $\Sigma_{2x} = \text{Re }\Sigma_{2x}(k_{\text{F}}, k_{\text{F}}^2/2)$ , is given by a certain integral. This integral is treated here in a similar way as Onsager, Mittag, and Stephen [Ann. Physik (Leipzig) 18, 71 (1966)] have obtained their famous analytical expression $e_{2x} = \frac{1}{6} \ln 2 - \frac{3}{4} \frac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}$ (in atomic units) for the correlation energy in second order of exchange. Here it is shown that the result for the corresponding on-shell self-energy is $\Sigma_{2x} = e_{2x}$ . The off-shell self-energy $\Sigma_{2x}(k,\omega)$ correctly yields $2e_{2x}$ (the potential component of $e_{2x}$ ) through the Galitskii-Migdal formula. 

The quantities $e_{2x}$ and $\Sigma_{2x}$ appear in the high-density limit of the Hugenholtz-van Hove (Luttinger-Ward) theorem.

content.title: Exact first-order density matrix for a d-dimensional harmonically   confined Fermi gas at finite temperature
content.text:
# Exact first-order density matrix for a *d*-dimensional harmonically confined Fermi gas at finite temperature

Brandon P. van Zyl

Department of Physics and Astronomy, McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, L8S 4M1

We present an exact closed form expression for the *finite temperature* first-order density matrix of a harmonically trapped ideal Fermi gas in any dimension. This constitutes a much sought after generalization of the recent results in the literature, where exact expressions have been limited to quantities derived from the diagonal first-order density matrix. We compare our exact results with the Thomas-Fermi approximation (TFA) and demonstrate numerically that the TFA provides an excellent description of the first-order density matrix in the large-N limit. As an interesting application, we derive a closed form expression for the finite temperature Hartree-Fock exchange energy of a two-dimensional parabolically confined quantum dot.

Time-dependent orbital-free density functional theory (DFT) is an efficient method for calculating the dynamic properties of large-scale quantum systems due to the low computational cost compared to standard time-dependent DFT. We formalize this method by mapping the real system of interacting fermions onto a fictitious system of noninteracting bosons. The dynamic Pauli potential and associated kernel emerge as key ingredients of time-dependent orbital-free DFT. Using the uniform electron gas as a model system, we derive an approximate frequency-dependent Pauli kernel. Pilot calculations suggest that space nonlocality is a key feature for this kernel. Nonlocal terms arise already in the second-order expansion with respect to unitless frequency and reciprocal space variable (ωqkF and q2kF, respectively). Given the encouraging performance of the proposed kernel, we expect it will lead to more accurate orbital-free DFT simulations of nanoscale systems out of equilibrium.

content.text: Here we propose a parametrization of this function based upon the satisfaction of exact constraints. For the static ( $\omega = 0$ ) limit, we modify the model of Constantin and Pitarke at small wavevector q to recover the known second-order gradient expansion, plus other changes. For all frequencies $\omega$ at q = 0, we use the model of Gross, Kohn, and Iwamoto. A Cauchy integral extends this model to complex $\omega$ and implies the standard Kramers-Kronig relations. A scaling relation permits closed forms for not only the imaginary but also the real part of $f_{xc}$ for real $\omega$ . We then combine these ingredients by damping out the $\omega$ dependence at large q in the same way that the q dependence is damped. Away from q = 0 and $\omega = 0$ , the correlation contribution to the kernel becomes dominant over exchange, even at $r_s = 4$ , the valence electron density of metallic sodium.

content.text:
Figure \(\PageIndex{1}\): The Thomas-Fermi atom consists of a nuclear charge \(+Ze\) surrounded by \(N\) electrons distributed in a cloud. The electric potential \(\phi(\Br)\) felt by any electron at position \(\Br\) is screened by the electrons within this radius, resulting in a self-consistent potential \(\phi(\Br)=\phi_0+(Ze^2/r)\,\xhi(r/r_0)\). At short distances, the nucleus is unscreened, \[\xhi(0)=1\ .\] For positive ions, with \(N<Z\), there is perfect screening at the ionic boundary \(R=t^*\,r\ns_0\), where \(\xhi(t^*)=0\). This requires \[\BE=-\bnabla\phi=\left[ -{Ze^2\over R^2}\,\xhi(R/r\ns_0) + {Ze^2\over R\,r\ns_0}\,\xhi'(R/r\ns_0)\right]\,\rhat = {(Z-N)\,e\over R^2}\,\rhat\ .\] This requires \[-t^*\,\xhi'(t^*)=1-{N\over Z}\ .\] For an atom, with \(N=Z\), the asymptotic solution to the TF equation is a power law, and by inspection is found to be \(\xhi(t)\sim C\,t^{-3}\), where \(C\) is a constant.



One important application of Thomas-Fermi screening is to the theory of metals. In a metal, the outer, valence electrons of each atom are stripped away from the positively charged ionic core and enter into itinerant, plane-wave-like states. These states disperse with some \(\ve(\Bk)\) function (that is periodic in the Brillouin zone, under \(\Bk\to\Bk+\BG\), where \(\BG\) is a reciprocal lattice vector), and at \(T=0\) this energy band is filled up to the Fermi level \(\veF\), as Fermi statistics dictates. (In some cases, there may be several bands at the Fermi level, as we saw in the case of yttrium.) The set of ionic cores then acts as a neutralizing positive background. In a perfect crystal, the ionic cores are distributed periodically, and the positive background is approximately uniform. A charged impurity in a metal, such as a zinc atom in a copper matrix, has a different nuclear charge and a different valency than the host.

eps_c^S(r_s,zeta) = eps_ring(r_s,zeta)/2 + eps_2x^scr(r_s,zeta)   [Ha]
 - eps_ring: the chain's own ring table (ring_table.json, BRM 2024 integrand, 41 r_s x 11 zeta) — unchanged.
 - eps_2x^scr: the second-order exchange diagram with ONE Coulomb line replaced by the coupling-constant-averaged statically screened line
   W(q) = v(q)/eps_L(q,0;lambda), eps_L the Lindhard static dielectric function of the SAME gas (the ring's own screening; Lindhard 1954), the average
   (1/1)∫_0^1 dlambda over the coupling constant as in the adiabatic connection (Gruneis-Kresse 2009 form; Ren et al 2013). No parameter enters: k_F, k_TF
   are functions of (r_s, zeta) alone. Spin: same-spin pairs only (the diagram); zeta enters through the two Fermi spheres and through eps_L(zeta).
 - Attribution: Onsager-Mittag-Stephen 1966 (bare constant, the kappa->0 limit); Ziesche 2006 (on-shell form); SOSEX: Gruneis-Kresse-Harl-Schimka 2009 /
   Ren-Rinke-Scheffler 2013; the reduction route (rescale frequency, factor denominators) 2603.23283 (2026, single-pole reference — NOT the physical screening).
## Gates (must fail if wrong)
 G-S1 kappa -> 0 (lambda-average off, bare v): reproduces E0B = 0.0241792 Ha to 1e-4 at zeta=0 AND zeta=1 (the ζ-independence of the bare diagram, FINDING-E0B).
 G-S2 r_s -> 0 (screening -> 0 in units of k_F): eps_c^S -> eps_c^R -> eps_c^Z (chain form) at r_s 1e-3 to 3e-5 Ha (gate 44 already fixes R = Z there).
 G-S3 the reduced integral agrees with a brute Monte-Carlo of the 9-D form to its statistical error at (r_s, zeta) = (2, 0) and (2, 1) — one point each, no scan.
## Predictions (write PREDICTION-SOSEX-SESSION-32.md BEFORE the first run; numbers below are the design's own expectation, entered there as PS-1..4)
 PS-1 eps_2x^scr(2,0)/E0B in [0.60, 0.80] (30 % reduction at r_s 2 needed to close R - bench +0.007);  PS-2 the reduction is monotone in r_s and larger at zeta=1
 than at zeta=0 at fixed r_s (a single Fermi sphere screens harder);  PS-3 form S against the RECALLED benchmark (comparison only): |S - bench| <= 0.003 Ha for
 r_s in [1,5] both spins — i.e. within the RPA+SOSEX literature accuracy;  PS-4 on the 15 chain rows (corr='S' hook, same interface as R): the nd>=4 rows deepen by
 0.004-0.006 relative to R and the 3d rows by <= 0.002, the 4f rows by <= 0.001 (rz_mech dR_loc as the bound) — the d-row object closes to <= 0.002; Sc goes to
 ~1.27 delivered and STAYS the anomaly (a 3d property, not a correlation-form property).
## Cost and order
 Build (reduced 3-4 dim quadrature) ~ one session's budget; batches; per-point cost must be measured before the 41 x 11 table is scheduled (a table of the SOX
 term at the ring grid; small-r_s below the table = E0B x reduction factor -> E0B). Then corr_sosex.py (E table + gradients as corr_ring), then t7c_corrz corr='S',
 15 rows both SUBCELL=1, COMPARE-RZS. Only after that: the walk test (SPEC-WALK) and the 4f/Yb item.
EOF
cat > pack31/SPEC-WALK-SESSION-32.md <<'EOF'
# SPEC — the walk test: is the Z -> Z+1 increment of the entrant IE a sum of derived mechanism increments, flat inside a shell and jumping at the shell edge?
# Written s31 (M: "a tree of mechanisms/truncations beginning at hydrogen"). Record: LCP3 Rule B (charge 1 over the previous configuration) 87/106, set aside
# because the neutral-core object under-binds the collapsing orbital; M's T0 ruling (LCP10) "consistent throughout ... by the walk/step functions"; R 1374 the
# walk is one of the three atomic ladders of Z = N_e + c - 1. Prior art: Bohr 1922 Aufbau; Slater 1930; Clementi-Raimondi 1963; Latter 1955; TIM 1986; Berengut.
## Object
 For consecutive rows held at chain quality: dIE(Z->Z+1) = sum_m d_m, m in {SR, x, SIC (beta_nl dN_sib + direct), SO/Hund-II, corr (window shift)}, each d_m the
 difference of the banked per-row mechanism contributions (no new physics; bookkeeping of what the chain already computes per row) + residual increment d_res.
## Predictions (to PREDICTION-WALK before the first read; the rows are already banked, so the read IS the run — timing discipline: write first)
 PW1 inside 4f: Dy->Er->Tm->Yb d_res flat to <= 0.01 (the +0.09-0.10 constant); PW2 inside 3d: Sc->Ti->(Cr)->Fe->Ni->Cu d_res NOT flat — it scatters with the
 term (the s27 finding restated as an increment) — until term-resolved SCF; PW3 the increment d_SIC inside a shell equals beta_nl (0.0044 4f, ~0.007 3d) per
 added sibling to 20 %; PW4 at a shell edge (Cu->[Zn]->Ga not banked; use Lu->[Hf] or Cs->[Ba]->La as the available edge) at least one d_m changes sign.
## Cost: reading and one table; no SCF. Gated on the correlation form (S) being ruled, because d_corr is one branch.
EOF
cd rt && ls | wc -l; cd .. && for f in $(ls rt); do [ "$f" = "__pycache__" ] && continue; case "$f" in *.so) continue;; esac; ls pack*/$f pack*/*/$f >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT IN PACK: $f"; done

content.text: Can the Maxwell equations help us better understand the electron behaviors we are trying to contain mathematically?

chat_messages.text:
Maxwell's equations are already implicit throughout this chain — Coulomb interaction is electrostatics, the Breit/spin-orbit terms bring in magnetism and retardation, and Lindhard screening is really the dielectric function of the electron gas, a Maxwell-in-a-medium object. The RPA ring diagrams capture exactly how the electron gas responds to its own field, giving rise to plasmons through ε(q,ω).…Yes, in one specific place, and it is the place we are standing.

The chain already contains Maxwell twice without naming him. The Coulomb term is Gauss's law; the spin-orbit and Hund-II pieces are the magnetic side (Ampère–Faraday, through Breit). What we have not used explicitly is the third thing Maxwell gives: the electron gas as a *medium*, with a dielectric function ε(q, ω). The RPA ring is exactly that — the electrons responding to the field they make themselves — and the Lindhard function is Maxwell's ε written for a Fermi sea. So the difference R − Z that this session isolated is the Maxwell part of correlation, resummed; and the missing piece of both forms, the screening of the second-order exchange, is Maxwell applied to the exchange line: the exchanged photon travels through the medium, not through vacuum. Candidate S is, in that language, "let the Pauli term see the field the gas has already dressed." That is a clearer statement of what SPEC-SOSEX is doing than the diagram language, and I'd put it in the spec.

It also gives us gates that can fail with no constants: the f-sum rule and the compressibility sum rule are Kramers–Kronig consequences of causality on ε(q, ω). Our ring table can be checked against them directly. That is a real, cheap addition to G-S1–3.

Where Maxwell cannot help: the branch that is statistics, not field. Exchange, SIC, the node count, 2(2ℓ+1) — antisymmetry has no field-theoretic image at the level we work. The chain's tree therefore splits cleanly into three trunks: electrostatic (Hartree, screening, corepol — Sternheimer is a Maxwell response computation), magnetic (SO, Hund-II, SR through Dirac), and statistical (Pauli, exchange, SIC). Correlation is the statistical trunk dressed by the electrostatic one — which is why it took two truncations to see it was one object. That three-way split may be a better spine for the law statement than "a chain of corrections."

I would not open any of it now; the sealed handoff stands. Two owed additions for the next session's spec: name the Lindhard ε as Maxwell's ε in the medium in SPEC-SOSEX, and add the two sum rules as gates.
